## Cast audit and XLSX private-store follow-up — 2026-10-18

The targeted cast review found `packages/io-xlsx/src/import.ts` reading and writing the private `Worksheet.cells` map through `(this as any)` to attach imported formulas. `LazyWorksheet` is private, and public `importXLSX()` already throws before creating a candidate workbook, but the bypass still skipped the raw Worksheet ownership guard if reached. It now calls `this.setCellFormula(addr, cell.formula)`, matching the existing guarded value/style calls. The two matching semantic records (`d7a86d01a3409e3ddba0`, `160185ac8bf980fce0ab`) are recorded `partial-owner-split`: R2/R5 writes remain unavailable and public restore remains R6-gated. The direct raw-store cast is absent from `import.ts`.

The full `io-xlsx` Jest command was run and exited `1` before assertions (0 tests executed). Both discovered suites fail during `ts-jest` compilation because existing tests still call mutators on `WorkbookSheetView`; `integration-hardening-sprint.test.ts` also has a pre-existing `FormulaEngine`/`IFormulaEngine` type mismatch. No tests were skipped or weakened. These cases exercise workbook writes and XLSX restore, so they remain implementation/test-migration findings for the unpublished R1/R2/R6 integration; they are not reported as passing.

This is a targeted cast disposition, not closure of the 153-line scan. Remaining casts in parser regex handling, DOM/canvas feature detection, event narrowing, and renderer interop still need callsite classification; workbook-relevant casts remain open unless joined to a keyed record and reviewed.

### ChartManager query and event contract audit — 2026-10-19

The implementation deliberately exposes live manager-local chart references today: `ChartManager.get()` returns the map entry, `getAll()` returns an array of those entries, derived queries filter the same objects, mutation methods return cached objects, and `emitEvent()` forwards its event/payload references. `saveChartsToMetadata()` explicitly documents that query results and event payloads refer to the local map and persists a JSON-cloned snapshot. The mutable `ChartObject`/`ChartEvent` types and the existing retained-query regression agree with this behavior. This establishes implementation intent for live references, but there is no separate public API contract specifying whether that behavior is supported after worksheet adoption.

Consumer trace: `ChartInteractionManager` uses chart identity (`id`) to call manager mutation methods and reads query results for hit-testing, hover, drag/resize setup, and rendering. Its manager event listener uses only the chart ID to invalidate/remove renderer cache entries and request redraw. `ChartRenderer` reads chart position, size, selection, range, series direction, and options; its render cache is refreshed through manager events. Framework ChartBuilder adapters forward only `event.chart.id`. `exportToJSON()` serializes the current map. No traced in-repository consumer mutates a returned query/event object to implement intended chart operations; supported interaction uses manager methods.

Focused regressions now cover retained create-event payload mutation across adoption for nested `metadata`, nested `options.colors`, `position`, `size`, `dataRange`, and `seriesDirection`. They confirm that manager hit-testing, interaction hover, and JSON export observe the changed local state while the worksheet metadata snapshot remains detached. They also characterize the consequence: direct alias mutation emits no manager event, so the interaction manager does not request redraw or invalidate its chart render cache. This makes live references observable implementation behavior, while showing that mutation through aliases bypasses validation, explicit persistence, event notification, and render invalidation. The contract is therefore still unresolved for a stable public API, especially for retained references across adoption; no production alias policy was changed and no ledger disposition was added.

### Strict ChartManager cloning contract — 2026-10-19

Resolved the helper's accessor/prototype ambiguity by defining chart inputs, cached values, and snapshots as strict JSON-compatible data. Accepted values are `null`, strings, booleans, finite numbers, dense ordinary arrays, and plain objects whose own properties are enumerable writable data properties. Plain objects may have `Object.prototype` or a null prototype. Shared but acyclic references are copied without retaining caller aliases.

The boundary rejects `undefined`, functions, symbols, bigint, non-finite numbers, accessors, non-enumerable or non-standard descriptors, symbol keys, sparse/custom-property arrays, custom object prototypes (including Date/Map/Set/binary objects), and cycles. The validation walks property descriptors and does not invoke getters. Since `create()` and `update()` clone and validate before changing the map, metadata, or emitting events, unsupported graphs fail atomically. Metadata reload rejects/skips an invalid chart rather than inserting its graph into the manager cache. `clone()` and JSON import omit absent optional title/metadata fields instead of constructing own `undefined` fields that violate the data contract.

Regressions exercise accessor-backed, custom-prototype, Date, non-enumerable, and cyclic metadata; verify getter non-invocation; and confirm failed create/update attempts leave manager exports, counts, metadata, and events unchanged. Existing input/output and listener-isolation cases continue to cover nested position, size, range, options, series direction, and metadata. This is a data-contract restriction for ChartManager chart values, not a general metadata serialization redesign.

### CanvasRenderer shallow options and sheet getter audit — 2026-10-19

Reviewed the module and exact semantic keys `78ad5d4e630576e8448c` (RenderLayer callback sheet type), `f68d66f22807aa296e05` (stored sheet type), `e11a689e9d6c4221bc7a` (constructor source), and `e00e049141e55ab4bac7` (`sheetReadonly`). All remain open; the module remains `partial-owner-split`.

`optionsReadonly` returns `this.options` itself. The `Readonly` wrapper is shallow and compile-time-only: callers receive the live wrapper, whose primitive settings can be reassigned at runtime, and whose `theme`, callback, worker/factory, image array or provider, and `drawingLayer` references are retained. `images` and `drawingLayer` are read during later rendering; changing the returned wrapper can also replace those references without updating the original drawing-layer subscription. These are live renderer configuration aliases, not detached observations. `getViewportSize()` returns a fresh scalar-only object. `onRequestColumnFilterMenu` callbacks receive a fresh anchor and value list plus apply/clear closures; the retained closures call the ownership-guarded mutation path. `onRender` receives a copied regions array, though its nested region objects are not deeply copied; callback payload review remains open.

`sheetReadonly` returns the exact object stored by the renderer. A renderer built with a `WorkbookSheetView` keeps the owner-backed view, whose cell reads detach values and mask formula cached values. A renderer built with a standalone `Worksheet` retains that raw handle if the worksheet is adopted later; writes through it reject, as covered by the existing renderer regression, but reads still use raw Worksheet semantics. In particular, `Worksheet.getCellValue()` returns the stored cell value while `WorkbookSheetView.getCellValue()` returns `null` for formula cells. The contrast is established by source review plus the existing core view formula-masking regression; no renderer-specific formula comparison was run. The constructor also accepts an already adopted raw `Worksheet` because its auto-size guard distinguishes by `instanceof Worksheet`, not ownership. Thus the getter is a raw capability when its source is a Worksheet and is not a detached snapshot.

`RenderLayer.draw` receives the same stored sheet and a `getScroll` closure. Existing `renderer.test.ts` coverage confirms the retained getter and callback sheet remain the raw Worksheet after adoption and that post-adoption writes reject before worksheet state changes. The separate drawing-layer regression confirms a supplied pre-adoption layer remains a detached standalone alias after Worksheet adoption. It does not establish deep immutability of options, image inputs, or every callback payload.

### Bounded forwarded formula-query correction — 2026-10-19

Applied a narrow fail-closed policy to forwarded Worksheet queries whose results could depend on adopted formula cached values. On a standalone Worksheet, `getDistinctValues`, `find`/`findAll`/`findIterator`, `getSpecialCells`, and filtered-row queries continue to use the existing Worksheet behavior. On an adopted Worksheet observation handle, distinct-value queries reject when a formula in the result column or an applicable visible-only filter could affect the output; value searches reject when formula cells are in the search range; and formula-value/error special-cell queries reject when formulas in range could affect matches. Formula text searches remain available because their formula-cell result is derived from formula text. Filtered-row queries reject only when an active filter column intersects an in-range formula cell.

The WorkbookSheetView's existing `findAll` now rejects value searches when formula cells in range could affect matches. Its filtered-row queries apply the same active-filter/formula intersection guard before delegating; excluding a filter column still works when that removes the only formula-dependent filter. This avoids returning formula-cache-dependent results where the view has no equivalent authorized query semantics. `evaluateIfNeeded` and `evaluateBatch` remain guarded owned mutations. No workbook write, automatic freshness behavior, general Worksheet proxy API, or new query API was introduced.

Regressions verify standalone query behavior, fail-closed behavior through a retained renderer handle and WorkbookSheetView, safe formula-text search, and the indirect filtered-row/visible-only distinct-value path. ### CanvasRenderer plugin callback and retained-reference audit — 2026-10-19

Reviewed the CanvasRenderer plugin invocations against semantic keys `26f4e0adc0d94c42507c` (`getCellValue`), `7d5b73438265cfe4b6fa` (`getCellStyle`), and `35324691bf2acc474589` (`isRowLoaded`, formerly through an `any` receiver). RenderPlugin callbacks are invoked from the cell render path at current source lines 2177, 2203, 2270, 2380, 2405, and 2709. Each invocation builds a fresh context with `createRenderPluginContext()`. The helper detaches the address, cell value, and style recursively for each call; the callback can mutate or retain those objects without changing the renderer's local address, worksheet cell value, or worksheet style. The `afterCellRender` hook also receives a newly constructed rectangle. It intentionally receives the live `CanvasRenderingContext2D`, which grants drawing authority over the renderer canvas but does not expose a Worksheet handle.

Before adoption, a standalone Worksheet source may provide the existing formula cached value to a plugin context. Once the source is workbook-owned, the CanvasRenderer observation proxy masks formula cached values on subsequent reads; an owner-backed `WorkbookSheetView` also returns `null` for formula-cell values. A context retained from before adoption remains a detached copy of data already observed at that time; mutation of that copy cannot change owner state, and ownership transition cannot revoke information already delivered. No callback parameter contains the renderer's stored Worksheet or its proxy/view object.

The plugin object itself is a retained, mutable extension capability: `addPlugin()` stores it, `getPlugin()` returns that same object, and later renders invoke its current callback properties. A plugin can also close over references supplied by its caller. These behaviors allow plugin configuration and caller-defined side effects; they do not originate in the callback context and this review found no renderer-supplied Worksheet handle path through them. Callback return values are consumed for rendering only: background/color/font results feed canvas style fields, and `afterCellRender`'s return is ignored. No callback return value is stored as Worksheet state.

One out-of-contract input edge remains open. `ExtendedCellValue` excludes functions, but `Worksheet.setCellValue()` assigns its typed argument without runtime value validation, and `detachRenderPluginValue()` returns functions unchanged because they are non-object values. Therefore a function inserted through an unchecked cast could be handed to a plugin by identity and carry its own closure effects. This is not demonstrated by a supported typed cell value or by a runtime regression, and it does not itself prove a workbook-owner mutation escape; it remains a runtime input-validation and plugin-trust question. This audit added no tests and made no source changes.

The callback context evidence is refreshed on the three exact semantic keys above; all three dispositions remain as recorded (one `partial-owner-split`, two `open-not-reconciled`). ### ExcelApp context-menu Paste source-only follow-up — 2026-10-22

The right-click handler assigns `contextMenuSelectionRef.current` from the first value returned by `renderer.getSelections()`, falling back to `renderer.selection` or React `selection`. `CanvasRenderer.getSelections()` and `ExcelRenderer.getSelections()` shallow-copy their selection arrays only; ExcelApp retains the selected range object and nested address objects without cloning/freezing them. The listener separately stores the hit-tested cell in `contextMenuTargetCellRef`. If the hit is inside the captured range, it updates `selectedCell` without shrinking or replacing that range.

The context-menu Paste item reads `contextMenuSelectionRef.current` and calls `pasteAtSelection()` with that range. `pasteAtSelection()` resolves the then-current `workbook.activeSheet` and sends `sel.start` as the paste anchor to `performPasteAsync()`. ### CanvasRenderer observation-handle exact-key reconciliation — 2026-10-23

Compared current `CanvasRenderer.ts` against the 2026-10-19 [Worksheet API inventory](../../../../../.cache/cs002d4-r1-evidence/implementation-reconciliation/canvasrenderer-observation-handle-review-2026-10-19/worksheet-api-inventory.tsv) and [owner-method review](../../../../../.cache/cs002d4-r1-evidence/implementation-reconciliation/canvasrenderer-observation-handle-review-2026-10-19/owner-method-review.md). The four exact records are `78ad5d4e630576e8448c` (RenderLayer callback sheet type), `f68d66f22807aa296e05` (retained `#sheet` type), `e11a689e9d6c4221bc7a` (constructor input), and `e00e049141e55ab4bac7` (`sheetReadonly` exposure). All remain `open-not-reconciled`; the CanvasRenderer module remains `partial-owner-split`.

**Current source boundary.** `RenderLayer.draw` receives `Worksheet | WorkbookSheetView`; the renderer stores the same union in ECMAScript-private `#sheet`; the constructor accepts either type, wraps raw Worksheet inputs with `createWorksheetObservationHandle()`, and leaves WorkbookSheetView inputs as owner views; `sheetReadonly` returns that stable stored handle. For raw Worksheet sources, the Proxy intercepts `isWorkbookOwned`, `getCell`, `getCellByKey`, `getCellValue`, `forEachNonEmptyCell`, and seven formula-sensitive query methods. Other methods are fetched from the raw target and function values are bound to it. The implementation therefore provides a selected observation facade, not a complete Worksheet API translation to WorkbookSheetView.

**Existing evidence and resolved subpaths.** The retained-proxy regressions cover selected formula-read parity through adoption, standalone write forwarding, adopted write rejection, constructor timing, and reflective non-exposure of `#sheet`. Focused tests also establish that `canonicalStyle()` remains available standalone and rejects on adopted raw and renderer handles before StyleCache metrics change; this closes that specific owner-cache mutation path. `queryPivotDataAt()` forwards to the owner callback after adoption and returns the scalar `GetPivotDataResult`; the owner GETPIVOTDATA path calls this Worksheet method. These observations do not demonstrate exposure of the Workbook object or pivot registry itself.

**Forwarded contracts still unresolved.** `onMutation()` remains dynamically forwarded although it is absent from WorkbookSheetView. Tests establish standalone subscription/delivery/disposal and that registrations can be made after adoption; tested public writes then reject before notification. No authorized owner-internal mutation path exercises delivery to an adopted subscription, so payload isolation, owner-side lifecycle, and event-order semantics remain unverified (the latter also depends on R4). The owner-query policy for `queryPivotDataAt()` also remains undecided because this owner service is callable on the renderer observation handle but is absent from WorkbookSheetView. These are capability/API questions, not demonstrated Workbook data mutation escapes.

The API inventory also records forwarded scalar or newly constructed diagnostics (`dirtyCount`, `dagStats`, `volatileCount`, `isTransactionActive()`, `isProgressiveLoading()`, `isDirty()`, and `getRecalculationPlan()`). Their current source returns do not by themselves establish a mutable alias, but those internal calculation/lifecycle observations are absent from WorkbookSheetView and have not been reconciled as an owner-view contract. Numerous other getters are present on the proxy but not the owner view; earlier bounded getter work covers selected detached results only and does not provide blanket closure for the inventory. Formula-sensitive query guards cover the specifically intercepted methods, subject to their implemented fail-closed conditions; they do not prove all forwarded reads are formula-safe. Separately recorded worker flows remain open where worker gates dynamically dispatch `isWorkbookOwned()`; the proxy’s captured ownership check for its intercepted reads does not settle those worker boundaries.

No distinct material gap requiring a new test or production change was established by this source comparison. No tests were run. The four semantic dispositions and module disposition are unchanged, no frozen register was modified, and R1 acceptance remains withheld.

**Access and delivery.** `onMutation()` is an `@internal` Worksheet method, but it remains a runtime method. `CanvasRenderer.sheetReadonly` returns the stable raw-Worksheet observation Proxy for Worksheet inputs, and the Proxy dynamically forwards unlisted methods bound to the raw target. Consequently a retained renderer handle can register or dispose an `onMutation()` listener after adoption; prior `renderer.test.ts` characterization confirms this, while `WorkbookSheetView` does not expose the method. The four relevant frozen semantic records remain `78ad5d4e630576e8448c` (RenderLayer callback source), `f68d66f22807aa296e05` (retained `#sheet`), `e11a689e9d6c4221bc7a` (constructor source), and `e00e049141e55ab4bac7` (`sheetReadonly`). They cover the path by which the capability is retained/exposed, but none names the `onMutation()` call or Worksheet emitter itself.

`Worksheet.#_emitOrBuffer()` is the sole source-level fanout point found. It invokes mutation listeners synchronously before adding the event to transaction pending events or emitting/coalescing the public event. Its events are produced by Worksheet mutation operations. The production `TransactionContext` and `PatchRecorder` consumers use `onMutation()` on the `SpreadsheetEngine`/worker-owned standalone Worksheet path; the `Workbook.create()` path subscribes to `sheet.on()`, not `onMutation()`. The experimental `WorkbookCalculationPrototype` also subscribes, but remains isolated and non-exported. The closest frozen ownership-flow records are `43979bb16c6e12564092` (`PatchRecorder` calling `applyPatch`) and `4ba92f4429227d58d84f` (`TransactionContext` rollback calling `applyPatch`). They cover patch mutation paths, not an adopted Workbook delivery path. No frozen semantic or flow record specifically covers listener registration or `#_emitOrBuffer()` delivery; no new key is assigned.

**Payloads and callback influence.** For an owned Worksheet, each registered wrapper independently calls `detachOwnedEventValue(event)` before invoking its listener. The source recursively copies and freezes supported event data and removes function values, so one subscriber cannot mutate the event object observed by the next subscriber. Standalone subscriptions intentionally receive the original event object under current source behavior. This is a source-level conclusion; the runtime characterization did not deliver an owner-generated event to multiple adopted subscriptions.

Listener invocation is not caught. A throwing listener can escape `#_emitOrBuffer()`, stop later listeners from running, and prevent that emitter call from reaching pending/public event publication. A reentrant listener can call Worksheet methods; on an adopted Worksheet, the registered mutation-entry guards reject the tested public writes, while standalone reentrant behavior remains ordinary Worksheet behavior. A registered callback remains reachable until its disposer is called; adoption does not revoke it. These are concrete callback semantics, but their effect on Workbook-owned mutation processing is conditional because R1 exposes no authorized owner-side mutation path that reaches this emitter. Existing adopted-subscription tests register and dispose listeners, then confirm public writes reject before event delivery. They do not resolve how a future authorized owner transaction should handle listener exceptions, reentrancy, or per-subscriber delivery.

**R1 and R4 boundary.** No current supported Workbook flow was found that both performs an owner-side Worksheet mutation and invokes an adopted `onMutation()` subscription. Therefore this review does not demonstrate a present owner-state write escape or a reachable event-delivery failure. The registration capability remains outside `WorkbookSheetView`, and its future owner policy is open. If a real authorized owner mutation route is introduced, the focused qualification should retain subscriptions through both raw and renderer handles, then use that real route to verify that one subscriber's mutable/retained payload, exception, or reentrant call cannot corrupt another subscriber's observation or the owner mutation. That test must be keyed to the four observation-handle semantic records above and to the exact owner mutation flow that supplies the real route; until such a route exists, there is no honest runtime test for owner delivery. Ordering/coalescing remains R4.

### `getRecalculationPlan()` exposure and reachability — 2026-10-23

Source-only follow-up compared the local plan output with the owner-view API and traced the supported renderer paths. `Worksheet.getRecalculationPlan()` returns fresh `addresses` and `cycles` arrays. The addresses are formula cells in the local dependency graph's evaluation order; cycle entries contain newly allocated sorted graph keys, unpacked row/column coordinates, and a message. The method checks formula metadata to filter the ordered graph nodes, but does not return formula text or cached formula results. Its address and cycle objects do not alias the graph.

`WorkbookSheetView` exposes detached `getFormulaAddresses()` and formula-bearing cell metadata with cached values masked. It does not expose dependency edges, dirty evaluation order, or cycle diagnostics. Thus the owner view can already identify formula coordinates, but not the plan's graph order or cycle grouping/diagnostic strings. That informational difference is source-established; no confidentiality consequence is demonstrated by these fields alone.

`Worksheet.adoptByWorkbook()` clones/replaces the drawing layer, sets the owner id, and prevents extensions; it does not replace or reset the Worksheet's `#dag` or `#recalcCoordinator`. An internally adopted raw Worksheet therefore retains the local graph state relevant to the plan. The normal `Workbook.create()` path instead constructs a fresh Worksheet and adopts it immediately; the reviewed Workbook-facing first-party React renderers obtain `WorkbookSheetView` from `getSheet()`/`activeSheet` and pass that view to `CanvasRenderer`. Their `sheetReadonly` and RenderLayer callback sheet therefore remain owner views, which do not provide `getRecalculationPlan()`. No first-party `RenderLayer` registration using a raw Worksheet was found. Raw Worksheet observation-handle access after adoption remains characterized only through the internal adoption seam, not a supported Workbook lifecycle.

Conclusion: the retained raw-backed renderer proxy can expose non-authoritative Worksheet-local graph order and cycle coordinates after internal adoption, while the supported first-party Workbook renderer path cannot reach that method. The extra graph details are absent from the owner-view contract, so the authorization policy remains an open contract dependency; source review does not establish an additional confidentiality failure or justify a runtime regression or implementation change. #### Current `import.ts` versus the exported OpenPanel loader

The frozen `import.ts` anchors no longer match the current executable source. `importXLSX()` currently throws `XLSX import is unavailable until R6 staged restore is authorized` at entry, before creating a Workbook or parser. `streamXLSX()` parses and yields cell chunks, and `previewXLSX()` returns metadata; neither creates or publishes a Workbook. `LazyWorksheet` is declared but not constructed in this module. Current `Workbook.addSheet()` unconditionally throws the sheet-lifecycle journal error, and `Workbook.getSheet(name)` returns `undefined` for an absent name. Thus the stale `new Workbook()`/getSheet/addSheet/getSheet flow in `import.ts` is not reachable as written.

OpenPanel imports `loadXlsxFromArrayBuffer()` from package-root `@cyber-sheet/io-xlsx`, implemented in sibling `packages/io-xlsx/src/index.ts`. That loader's gate enables import when `CYBER_SHEET_ENABLE_XLSX_IMPORT === '1'` or `__CYBER_SHEET_DEV__ === true`. The current Vite configuration sets the compile-time flag true for `mode === 'development'`; the development path is therefore reachable in the configured dev server. Other runtime/build environments can also enable it through the environment variable or by defining the compile-time constant true; enablement is not intrinsically limited to Vite. When disabled, the gate throws before unzip or Workbook construction.

When enabled, the sibling loader creates `new Workbook()`, creates each sheet with `createDevImportWorksheet()`, writes cell values and styles while the Worksheet is not adopted, then calls `attachDevImportSheet()`. That API stores the Worksheet in the Workbooks' private sheet maps and wires observation bridges but explicitly does not adopt it. The loader returns only after processing the sheet loop. Consequently, it returns a Workbook whose `getSheet()` and `activeSheet` still return `WorkbookSheetView` facades, but whose private backing Worksheets do not satisfy the adopted-storage invariant established by `Workbook.create()`. The view facade alone does not establish adopted backing state. The loader keeps no raw Worksheet reference in its return value; raw sheets remain in Workbook private storage. `createDevImportWorksheet()` and `attachDevImportSheet()` are public methods marked `@internal`; callers that use those seams can retain the raw Worksheet they supplied, but the loader itself does not return that reference.

#### Read and failure behavior

The development importer processes `<v>` cached cell content and optional styles through `setCellValue()`/`setCellStyle()` before attaching the sheet. It does not parse or call `setCellFormula()` for `<f>` formula metadata, nor does this path restore drawings or broader workbook metadata. A formula cell containing `<f>40+2</f><v>42</v>` is therefore stored as an ordinary value `42`; `WorkbookSheetView.getCellValue()` masks only cells that carry formula metadata, so the returned view can expose this imported cached result as an ordinary value. This is a source-established R1 read-isolation concern on the Vite-development path, not a runtime test result.

If unzip, XML processing, cell writing, or attachment throws, the loader does not return the local Workbook and OpenPanel does not call its publication callback. Any already attached partial sheet state remains confined to that local candidate graph; no raw Worksheet or parser object is forwarded by the loader. On success, OpenPanel calls its callback only after loader return; ExcelApp can then pass the Workbook to the host and consume sheet reads through `WorkbookSheetView`. This post-return ordering prevents partial parse publication, but does not repair the unadopted backing storage or formula-cache-as-value issue. `importXLSX()`/progressive staged restore remain gated; the development loader is a distinct active path, not evidence that R6 restoration is complete.

### XLSX export ownership and formula-read reconciliation — 2026-10-23

Source-only review updated exactly the existing `packages/io-xlsx/src/export.ts` module record, its eleven semantic records (`662a76c44d298e5f27d0`, `78ff2a1f32d34b4a5b63`, `970cc40c762381290f29`, `0435a29da6acbd06f138`, `c3171d652a068164f49d`, `920435930a75fcbb65af`, `0bd451ff9870af94f173`, `288dbe7ec9ea28709683`, `9889dc91ae6c8da3df36`, `f31496aacf708eae6254`, `e84541a7215778dbd237`), and seven flow records (`8e9bca5455febe3f5dd8`, `224080342b3206e03a17`, `db2f571e451759446a84`, `b71cd3aa0d5697b3ff4a`, `7ec3a9610d1e62002fff`, `02b8269032a0d3db641c`, `ff9fd7a9ec5f5750843d`). All remain at their existing dispositions; frozen identifiers and source anchors were not modified.

#### Workbook and standalone routes

`exportXLSX()` accepts `Workbook | Worksheet`. `exportSource()` passes a Workbook through as the `getSheetNames()`/`getSheet()` source interface. Workbook `getSheet()` returns `WorkbookSheetView`; first-party React `ExportPanel` and `CreateCopyPanel` both call the exporter with Workbook. On that route, `forEachNonEmptyCell()` provides detached cell observations, formula cells have their cached value masked to `null`, `getCellValue()` also returns `null` for formula cells, and `cell.formula` remains available. The generated XLSX preserves formula text in `<f>` but emits an empty cached `<v>`. Styles and cell values are read via public read methods; the Workbook path does not cast to Worksheet or inspect private owner storage.

For a `Worksheet` input, `exportSource()` wraps and returns the same Worksheet without checking whether it is standalone or already adopted. This preserves the intended standalone overload, but it also means an internally retained raw Worksheet can be passed after adoption. The raw Worksheet's adopted `getCell()` and `forEachNonEmptyCell()` return detached records, yet `getCellValue()` continues returning their cached formula value; detachment prevents a mutable cell alias but does not apply WorkbookSheetView's formula-result mask. `generateSheetXML()` reads both `cell.formula` and `sheet.getCellValue(address)`, so a retained adopted raw Worksheet with a formula and cache can serialize both the formula and cached result. This is a concrete internal retained-raw read path; no supported first-party React exporter caller supplying an adopted raw Worksheet was found, and the core package root does not export the internal adoption helper. It is not evidence of a first-party Workbook export escape.

The exporter does not call Worksheet/Workbook mutators. It creates local XML strings, byte arrays, and the final zip buffer; the async function contains no `await`, so it does not retain the source or cell observations across an asynchronous suspension or callback. Workbook metadata output is limited to sheet names/relationships/content types in the reviewed path.

#### Style projection qualification

`exportXLSX()` collects styles in a `Map<CellStyle, number>` keyed by object identity, then `generateSheetXML()` performs a second `getCellStyle()` read to look up the style index. WorkbookSheetView returns a newly detached style snapshot on each call. Source inspection therefore indicates that an owner-view style read in the second pass may not have the same identity as the first-pass key, leaving the cell without the expected style index in the emitted sheet XML. This is an export-fidelity concern, separate from owner-state mutation and not runtime-characterized in this source-only review. No change or test was authorized here.

#### Exact-key follow-up

The exact-key evidence distinguishes the normal Workbook view route, standalone Worksheet compatibility, and the internal retained-adopted-raw Worksheet route. If the retained-raw export behavior is to be characterized, a narrowly scoped regression can create a formula-bearing standalone Worksheet, retain it, pass it through the existing internal adoption test seam, and export that raw handle; inspect the emitted sheet XML for formula text and cached `<v>` value. Keep this separate from the supported Workbook route, whose view masks the cached result. The style-identity observation would require its own focused export-fidelity characterization if separately authorized. No production changes or tests were made/run under this source-only directive, and no disposition was promoted.

### ExportPanel first-party publication boundary — 2026-10-23

Source-only review updated exactly three existing ExportPanel records: the module, semantic key `5b619515c4252db99901`, and semantic key `185ccda28773f59b6274`. Their dispositions and frozen anchors remain unchanged.

The first-party route is `ExcelApp -> BackstageContainer -> ExportPanel`. ExcelApp's `workbook` prop is required and typed `Workbook`; the Backstage passes that same object to ExportPanel. The XLSX branch invokes `exportXLSX(workbook)` directly. The panel does not extract, retain, or publish a raw Worksheet. The export function returns an ArrayBuffer, which the panel wraps in a Blob. Its `onExportComplete` callback receives only Blob and format, not a Workbook or Worksheet capability. XLSX exports all sheets by passing the Workbook; the CSV branch instead intends to export only `workbook.activeSheet`.

Other format paths are distinct. PDF displays a print-dialog alert and returns without download or completion callback. ODS throws “coming soon”; TXT/HTML delegate to `FileOperations.exportWorkbook()`, whose current implementation throws “Export not yet connected to renderer”. CSV manually loops over 100 rows and 26 columns, starting at `{row: 0, col: 0}`. The owner view delegates reads to Worksheet, whose address assertion requires one-based row and column values, so the first CSV read throws `Worksheet address out of bounds: row=0, col=0; expected rows 1–1048576 and columns 1–16384.` The catch clears progress/loading and allows retry but silently displays no error; no Blob, download, success state, or callback is reached. CSV delimiter/header state is not consumed by this manual serializer. XLSX does not use CSV/PDF options.

There are two successful-completion publication concerns. First, ExportPanel itself creates and clicks a download link, then invokes `onExportComplete(blob, format)`. BackstageContainer drops `format` when forwarding the Blob to ExcelApp. ExcelApp then creates a second download named `${fileName}.xlsx` regardless of the selected format. This yields duplicate XLSX downloads and a mislabeled second download for any alternate format that successfully returns a Blob. Second, after export resolves, ExportPanel awaits a fixed 300ms delay before its local download and callback. Backstage changes the keyed panel subtree when switching panels, unmounting ExportPanel; its cleanup clears only the progress interval and does not cancel the pending continuation. Thus a panel can be switched/unmounted during that delay and still later trigger a download/callback and state updates. The source has no operation cancellation or mounted guard. Mouse format changes are blocked while exporting, but the format card keyboard handler does not check `isExporting`, so selection can change during an in-flight export while that operation continues with its captured format.

No tests were run for this source-only review. A focused characterization for the concrete stale-completion path would hold the 300ms completion timer, unmount/switch away from ExportPanel, then release the timer and observe whether download creation and `onExportComplete` still occur. The duplicate/mislabeled download path is also source-established; if separately characterized, capture link clicks through the ExcelApp -> BackstageContainer -> ExportPanel route for an XLSX selection and verify how many downloads receive the same Blob. No production change or disposition promotion is proposed here.

The export button is disabled while a request is active, so the ordinary UI does not start an overlapping newer export; the component has no cancel action. The keyboard handler can still change the selected format while exporting, but the in-flight handler retains the format captured when it started. This is a UI consistency issue, not a second export request.

### CreateCopyPanel ownership source review — 2026-10-23

Source-only trace: `ExcelApp` passes its required `Workbook` prop to `BackstageContainer`; the `createCopy` branch passes the same Workbook value to `CreateCopyPanel`. The panel invokes `exportXLSX(workbook)`, wraps the returned bytes in an XLSX Blob, and triggers a browser download named from `copyName + extension`. It does not create or publish an in-memory Workbook, call a host copy callback, or invoke a FileOperations copy method. The resulting Blob/download contains serialized bytes and does not retain a Worksheet capability. Because R6 import remains gated, this establishes a downloadable artifact, not a verified in-app Workbook restoration.

The displayed destination is not applied: `selectedLocation` is initialized from `currentLocation` and can be changed in the selector, but the create handler never reads it and always uses `URL.createObjectURL()` plus an anchor click for local browser download. `fileOperations` is accepted and passed but is unused by this handler. Filename extension follows the original filename, defaulting to `.xlsx`; the payload is always XLSX from `exportXLSX()`.

The create button, input, location selector, and Cancel button are disabled while `isCreating`; Enter also checks `!isCreating`, so the ordinary UI does not start overlapping requests. The callback awaits `exportXLSX(workbook)` and closes over that Workbook during the call. The current exporter performs its work synchronously before its Promise resolves; after resolution the panel uses only the ArrayBuffer/Blob, filename, and callbacks. The handler's dependency array omits `workbook`, although the actual ExcelApp caller supplies a freshly created inline `onClose` callback on rerender, which currently causes callback recreation when ExcelApp props change. Direct external CreateCopyPanel callers with a stable `onClose` could still retain a stale Workbook in the callback if the prop changes; no such route was established in this first-party trace.

Export failures are caught before Blob download, `isSuccess`, or the delayed close; the panel displays a generic retryable error and `finally` clears `isCreating`. After a successful download it sets success and schedules `onClose()` after 1.2 seconds. That timeout is not retained or cleared on unmount. Since Backstage's keyed panel container unmounts the panel when the active panel changes, a user can navigate elsewhere after the download but before the timeout fires, after which the stale timeout can still close Backstage. This is the concrete async lifecycle issue identified in this source review. A focused characterization would complete a copy, switch to another Backstage panel before 1.2 seconds elapse, then advance the timer and observe whether the stale `onClose` closes Backstage.

No CreateCopyPanel module, semantic, or flow record is assigned in the current implementation ledger or any of the three frozen R1 disposition registers. Accordingly, no key was invented or repurposed and no ledger evidence row or disposition was changed. The source trace is recorded here pending reconciliation of the frozen inventory. No tests or production edits were made.

### Backstage close/reopen session-generation correction — 2026-10-23

The preceding interrupted-close characterization remains as the pre-fix result: the same CreateCopyPanel instance survived the parent close/open request, the deferred old export published one Blob URL and one download click, and its original Back timer invoked the close callback at 200 ms, hiding the reopened panel.

`BackstageContainer` now advances a monotonically increasing Create Copy session generation when Back starts and when a new open session begins. ### ExportPanel source and publication-boundary review — 2026-10-23

Traced the first-party `ExcelApp -> BackstageContainer -> ExportPanel` route. ExcelApp conditionally mounts Backstage with its complete Workbook and an `onExportComplete` callback; Backstage forwards that Workbook unchanged to ExportPanel. The panel prop remains optional `any`, so external callers are not statically limited to Workbook, but no raw Worksheet ingress was found on the first-party route.

Format behavior in current source:

- XLSX calls `exportXLSX(workbook)`, which follows the complete Workbook/owner-view export path. It exports all Workbook sheets.
- CSV reads `workbook.activeSheet` for active-sheet-only output, but loops begin at `{row: 0, col: 0}`. The first owner-view `getCellValue()` call violates the one-based address contract and throws before producing a Blob. Its configured delimiter/header options are not used by the manual serializer.
- PDF clears progress, resets loading, and displays a browser-print alert; it returns before download or completion callback. The orientation/fit options are constructed but not applied in this branch.
- ODS throws its explicit not-implemented error. TXT/HTML delegate to `FileOperations.exportWorkbook()`, which currently throws `Export not yet connected to renderer`.

On any successful Blob branch, ExportPanel waits 300 ms, creates an object URL, clicks a local download link named from the Workbook filename and selected format, marks the UI complete, then calls `onExportComplete(blob, format)`. Backstage forwards the Blob to ExcelApp; ExcelApp independently creates another object URL and download click, hardcoding the `.xlsx` extension. Thus the currently reachable successful XLSX route initiates two downloads. Other formats currently exit before success, but the second-download callback would also use an `.xlsx` name if those paths later return Blobs. The UI disables the Download button during export, although the format-card keyboard handler can still change the displayed selected format; the in-flight handler retains the format captured when invoked.

A separate reachable lifecycle risk remains source-established. ExportPanel receives no Back close/session signal. Its unmount cleanup clears only the progress interval; it does not cancel the pending export or 300 ms completion delay. Switching panels unmounts the keyed ExportPanel subtree immediately, while Back/Escape leaves it mounted for the 200 ms exit transition. A resolved export can therefore continue after switch, after Back intent, or after unmount to download, update state, and call the parent completion callback. The catch path prevents download/callback on export failure but silently resets progress/loading without visible error feedback; the selected format remains available for retry. No runtime reproduction was performed in this source-only review.

The three existing ExportPanel records were refreshed individually in the implementation ledger: module, semantic `5b619515c4252db99901`, and semantic `185ccda28773f59b6274`. All dispositions remain `open-not-reconciled`; no frozen register identifiers changed.

A deferred-export case should resolve after panel switch and during/after the Back exit transition, then observe whether the unmounted panel still downloads or invokes `onExportComplete`. Keep duplicate publication and stale lifecycle observations distinct in the report. No production change is proposed by this source review. ### ExportPanel input contract source audit — 2026-10-23

Reviewed the ExportPanel prop declaration and all of its `workbook` reads, BackstageContainer's prop and forwarding, ExcelApp's first-party invocation, public package exports, and the runtime input assumptions of the XLSX and CSV paths. This is source-only; no runtime compatibility or arbitrary-caller test was run.

| Input/call boundary | Source-supported contract and use | Runtime validation / limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First-party `ExcelApp -> BackstageContainer -> ExportPanel` | `ExcelAppProps.workbook` is required and typed `Workbook`. ExcelApp passes that object through BackstageContainer unchanged; BackstageContainer forwards it to ExportPanel. The ExportPanel code comment calls it a Workbook instance. This is the established first-party input. | The instance is not checked with `instanceof Workbook`; the code relies on the first-party typed caller. On this path XLSX receives the Workbook and CSV reads its `activeSheet` owner view. |
| Standalone `Worksheet` | The public `exportXLSX()` signature expressly accepts `Workbook | Worksheet`, and its standalone Worksheet route is retained. ExportPanel's own prop comment does not document Worksheet compatibility. | XLSX can pass the standalone Worksheet through to the exporter. CSV expects `workbook.activeSheet`, so a Worksheet does not satisfy that input shape. No general ExportPanel standalone contract is established. An adopted raw Worksheet passed directly to the XLSX branch is rejected by the exporter's ownership predicate. |
| `WorkbookSheetView` | A view is a sheet-level read capability, not the Workbook-level object expected by either ExportPanel format path. | The XLSX exporter expects workbook-level `getSheetNames()`/`getSheet()` methods for non-Worksheet inputs. CSV expects an `activeSheet` property. ExportPanel does not wrap a view into a Workbook-like source. |
| Arbitrary structural object | `workbook?: any` allows TypeScript callers to pass any value, and the component is re-exported from the public React package barrel. BackstageContainer's `workbook?: any` is also publicly exported. | ExportPanel checks only for a falsy workbook. XLSX delegates to `exportXLSX()`, whose runtime check rejects a raw Worksheet only when the top-level argument is an actual Worksheet; other objects are treated as Workbook-like and used through `getSheetNames()`/`getSheet()`. CSV assumes `activeSheet`, dimensions, and `getCellValue()` capabilities. These checks validate neither Workbook identity nor ownership of objects returned by a structural adapter. Such shapes are not documented as supported. |

The checked first-party path demonstrates owner-backed reads; the public `any` props and package re-exports also make direct external component invocation possible. That availability establishes an input-contract gap, not by itself an ownership escape: a caller-provided structural object can expose its own read capabilities, while the reviewed Workbook API returns owner views and does not expose its private retained raw sheets. A structural XLSX adapter could evade the exporter's top-level `instanceof Worksheet` rejection if it already held and returned an adopted raw Worksheet, but this audit found no supported first-party route that gives such an alias to an external caller. The condition is a source-level guard limitation, not a reproduced or established external data disclosure.

No source states that ExportPanel supports standalone Worksheet, WorkbookSheetView, or arbitrary structural input. Tightening the public type to `Workbook`, or adding runtime identity/returned-sheet checks, could change the incidental standalone XLSX behavior and external component usage; choosing that contract requires a separate decision. For this review, accept only the typed first-party Workbook route as established, record standalone XLSX as underlying exporter capability rather than a panel-wide promise, and leave direct external input compatibility unresolved. ### React package-root packaging contract and correction assessment — 2026-10-23

Reviewed the React manifest and TypeScript build settings, repository build and CI checks, package-root imports in examples and documentation, the root Vite resolver, and the IO-XLSX dependency manifest. This is a source/configuration review only; no build, test, pack, or consumer probe was run in this subtask.

#### Existing packaging evidence

- `packages/react/package.json` is publishable (`private: false`) and includes `dist`; it declares `main` and `module` as `dist/index.js`, `types` as `dist/index.d.ts`, and has no `exports`, `publishConfig`, or package-specific bundler configuration. Its build script is `tsc -p tsconfig.json`.
- `packages/react/tsconfig.json` sets `outDir: "dist"`, `rootDir: "."`, declaration output, and inherits `module: "ES2020"` with `moduleResolution: "Bundler"`. With sources included only from `src`, that root setting explains the observed `dist/src/...` output. This is a TypeScript ESM build, not a package bundle.
- The CI build check explicitly requires `packages/react/dist/index.js`; this is direct repository evidence that the expected artifact layout is package-root `dist/index.js`. The development workflow simply runs the package's TypeScript build and has no separate packaging step.
- Product examples and docs use `@cyber-sheet/react` package-root imports in React UI examples. The root Vite config aliases that name to `packages/react/src/index.ts`, so those app builds exercise source through Vite rather than validating the published `dist` entry. The components target browser UI (React/DOM); the reviewed docs do not explicitly define a browser-bundler-only support boundary or promise native Node ESM/server-side rendering.
- The React manifest's `main` and `type: "module"` nevertheless advertise a Node-resolvable ESM package entry as well as the bundler-oriented `module` field. The consumer probes show that correcting only the missing root path would not by itself make the current extensionless emitted ESM imports load in native Node.
- `@cyber-sheet/io-xlsx` also declares `main`/`module`/`types` at `dist/index.*`; unlike React, its `tsconfig` uses `rootDir: "src"`, so its root files are emitted at those declared paths. Its emitted ESM still has extensionless relative imports (the direct React component probe failed while resolving `io-xlsx/dist/import`). That is a separate transitive native-Node compatibility issue, not the cause of React's own missing root files.

#### Candidate correction matrix

| Candidate | Files and expected effect | Potential regressions / limits | Evidence still needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Align React metadata with `dist/src` | Change `packages/react/package.json` `main`, `module`, and `types` paths. It would align all three declared paths with the current TypeScript output and likely let a bundler and TypeScript resolve the root files. | Contradicts CI's explicit `dist/index.js` check and leaves the source-rooted output layout exposed. It does not fix native Node's extensionless ESM resolution, including React-local and IO-XLSX imports. | Decide whether `dist/src` is the intended package layout; verify a packed consumer using the supported bundler and TypeScript; separately decide/test native Node expectations. |
| Change build output to package-root `dist` | Change `packages/react/tsconfig.json` `rootDir` from `.` to `src`, retaining `outDir: "dist"`; this emits `src/index` as `dist/index` and keeps paths relative to the source tree beneath `src`. It aligns `main`, `module`, `types`, and CI's expected root JS path without changing package metadata. | Changes every emitted relative path from `dist/src/...` to `dist/...`; may affect consumers of undocumented deep `dist/src` paths, build references, or stale artifacts. TypeScript still emits extensionless ESM specifiers, so native Node compatibility remains unresolved. | Run the React build and workspace build check after a separately authorized edit; inspect declaration maps and package contents; test packed TypeScript and browser-bundler consumers; decide whether Node ESM is promised. |
| Use package-oriented bundling | Add a library build configuration/script (and likely manifest adjustments) to emit explicit package-root JS/declarations, with dependencies and peer dependencies externalized deliberately. A bundler could rewrite/resolve React-local relative imports for the selected runtime target. | Broader change across `package.json` and build config; can alter chunking, CSS/assets, source maps, tree-shaking, peer dependency handling, subpath access, and declaration generation. Fixing React bundling alone does not fix native Node if `io-xlsx` remains an external dependency with incompatible emitted specifiers. | Establish target environments and supported subpaths; select bundler and externalization policy; verify full API/declaration surface, package contents, browser consumer, and Node/transitive dependency behavior if required. |
| Defer native Node ESM support | Document a browser-bundler-only runtime boundary and avoid claiming that the current emitted JS is directly executable by Node. This does not repair the missing package-root paths; it would need to accompany an entrypoint correction. | No existing documentation explicitly establishes bundler-only support, while `main` and `type: "module"` invite Node package resolution. Could exclude SSR, scripts, or other server-side React consumers. | Approve the runtime support contract; clarify the role of `main` versus `module`; validate the documented browser consumer from a packed artifact and ensure the chosen metadata does not continue to imply unsupported Node behavior. |

#### Recommendation

For the confirmed missing package-root entrypoints, recommend `rootDir: "src"` in `packages/react/tsconfig.json` as the smallest correction for a subsequent implementation decision. It matches the existing `main`/`module`/`types` paths and CI's explicit `dist/index.js` expectation while preserving the repository's TypeScript build approach. This recommendation is limited to emitted path alignment: it does not claim native Node ESM support, which remains a separate contract question because both React-local and IO-XLSX emitted imports are extensionless. The package docs/examples support browser-bundled usage, but the `main` field and lack of an explicit bundler-only statement leave the broader runtime contract unresolved. A packed browser/TypeScript consumer verification and an explicit Node support decision should precede or accompany implementation approval.

### Core formula-worker distribution contract review — 2026-10-23

This source-only review traces the default React worker construction against the current Core source, protocol, package exports, build command, and available distribution files. It changes no production source, configuration, tests, dependencies, ledger rows, or frozen registers.

**React construction path.** `packages/react/src/CyberSheet.tsx` creates the default worker lazily through `formulaWorkerFactory`, using `new Worker(new URL('../../core/src/worker/formula-worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })`, then wraps it in Core's `FormulaWorkerProxy`. A caller-supplied factory can replace this default path. The source-relative URL assumes the repository's sibling `react` and `core` source layout; it is not a package-stable location once React is built and consumed from packed artifacts. The earlier isolated packed Vite run confirms the practical consequence: Vite's worker URL handling requested `@cyber-sheet/core/src/worker/formula-worker.ts` from packed React `dist/CyberSheet.js` and failed with `UNRESOLVED_ENTRY`.

**Core runtime and protocol.** `packages/core/src/worker/formula-worker.ts` is a runtime entry: it imports `FormulaWorkerHost` and immediately installs its message listener. The host owns a worker-local `FormulaEngine` and standalone `Worksheet`; it handles `ping`, `setCellValue`, `setCellFormula`, `registerDeps`, and `evaluateBatch`, returning typed success/error responses. `evaluateBatch` transfers its result buffer back to the caller. `FormulaWorkerProxy` provides the corresponding main-thread request API and terminates the worker on disposal. These source files describe a functioning protocol implementation; they do not themselves establish that Core distributes an executable worker entry or that React's default URL is supported outside the monorepo.

**Package boundary and artifacts.** Core's `package.json` publishes `dist` and declares explicit root, `./sdk`, `./patch`, and `./snapshot` export paths; it has no worker subpath or worker factory export. `packages/core/src/index.ts` re-exports worker host, protocol, and proxy APIs from the package root, but that is not a separately addressable worker-entry URL. The Core build command bundles only `src/index.ts`, `src/sdk/index.ts`, `src/patch/index.ts`, and `src/persistence/SnapshotCodec.ts` through tsup; the subsequent TypeScript declaration-only pass emits worker declarations but not worker runtime JavaScript. The inspected `packages/core/dist/worker/` contains `.d.ts` and source-map files for the worker modules, including `formula-worker.d.ts`, but no `formula-worker.js`. Since the package's `files` list is `dist`, the source path requested by the packed React artifact is not included in the published package. Thus the observed Vite blocker is directly explained by an absent packaged runtime entry and the React source-relative reference. Merely adding a `./worker` export or copying declarations would not supply the executable file needed by `new Worker()`.

**Support-contract qualification.** The repository README labels off-thread formula calculation as “planned.” The implementation exists in source, but the inspected package metadata and documentation do not establish a supported default-worker distribution contract. The evidence therefore identifies the mechanical packaging gap without deciding that the planned worker must now become a supported public feature. If the product decision is to keep worker calculation planned, a distinct supported fallback/disable contract for React's default construction must be established. If the decision is to ship it, the smallest coherent implementation boundary is coordinated Core and React packaging: build and include an executable worker artifact at a stable package-consumer location, provide React a package-safe way to construct that artifact (or a stable Core factory), and remove the source-tree-relative URL. A public subpath is an option for defining that location, not by itself proof that worker URL resolution works.

**Smallest next implementation boundary and acceptance criteria.** Before production edits, decide whether the default formula worker is an intended supported distribution feature or remains unavailable/planned. For the supported-worker option, a bounded follow-up should change only the Core worker build/package surface and React default worker construction, preserving the existing message protocol and caller override. Acceptance should require: (1) a clean Core package build and packed tarball containing the actual worker JavaScript at its documented runtime path; (2) a clean React package build and packed-consumer resolution with no `core/src/worker` reference; (3) a Vite browser bundle from the real packed React/Core dependency graph that emits/resolves the worker asset without workspace-source fallback; and (4) a separately identified browser smoke test proving worker construction and a protocol round trip. Bundle success alone does not prove browser execution. If the worker remains planned, acceptance instead needs an explicit supported React behavior that avoids an unresolved default worker URL while keeping any caller-provided factory contract intact. Native Node ESM compatibility remains a separate runtime contract and should not be inferred from a successful browser-worker build. Any eventual Core artifact and React URL change should be reviewed and rolled back together; no protocol, Workbook ownership, or generic worker architecture change is implicated by this source review.

No build or Jest command was run for this source-only task. `git diff --check` was run after the report update and passed. Core worker distribution, full packed Vite bundling, browser execution, the worker support decision, and overall CS-002D4-R1 acceptance remain open.

### P0-01 default formula-worker distribution decision — recommendation

**Recommended option: the default formula worker is intentionally unavailable in the R1 React distribution; caller-supplied worker factories remain opt-in. This is a recommendation for review, not user sign-off or implementation authorization.**

Reasons: the README calls off-thread formula calculation planned; Core has no packaged runtime worker entry or worker export path; React's default URL reaches into a sibling source tree and fails in the packed Vite consumer; and `CanvasRenderer` already has a synchronous formula-evaluation path when no worker can be created. The source review did not establish an approved requirement to ship the worker now. Packaging the current URL or adding a subpath without a runtime artifact would not resolve the contract gap.

If approved, the supported R1 behavior should be: ordinary React package consumption does not require or attempt to resolve a Core source-tree worker; formula work uses the existing main-thread fallback where the renderer's current behavior permits it; applications may opt into a caller-provided `formulaWorkerFactory`, with construction, URL resolution, and lifecycle owned by that caller. This recommendation does not authorize changing CanvasRenderer fallback semantics or the worker protocol.

**Acceptance criteria for the bounded follow-up:**

1. The documented React default path creates no worker and contains no `core/src/worker` package dependency.
2. A focused renderer/React regression demonstrates ordinary formula rendering through the existing synchronous fallback and a separate control demonstrates that a caller-provided factory is still honored.
3. A clean packed React plus local-dependency Vite consumer bundle succeeds without resolving Core worker source, while retaining the prior pivot SDK resolution.
4. Typecheck, React build, full React Jest, and focused-test hygiene pass; the report records the exact toolchain, commands, warnings, and packed artifact graph.
5. No Core worker artifact, public worker export, protocol change, native Node ESM claim, or browser-worker smoke claim is included in this option.

If the product decision instead requires the default worker in R1, select the supported-worker option from the preceding source review and authorize the coordinated Core runtime artifact plus React package-safe URL/factory work before implementation. The P0-01 choice remains awaiting explicit review; Phase 1 code changes remain unauthorized, and R1 acceptance remains withheld.

- Package manifest inspection shows that React does not declare `@fluentui/react-icons` in `dependencies` or `peerDependencies`; neither `@cyber-sheet/icons` nor `@cyber-sheet/cf-ui-core` declares it. The import is part of React's own ribbon implementation, so React owns the direct runtime dependency declaration. It is an implementation dependency, not a consumer-supplied React peer contract.
- The root monorepo `package.json` declares `@fluentui/react-icons: "^2.0.337"`, and the root lockfile resolves it to 2.0.344. The React workspace lock entry has no Fluent UI dependency.
- The P1-02B offline consumer installed the six local workspace tarballs and then React's peer runtime packages. Neither its package list nor the React package dependency graph included `@fluentui/react-icons`. Thus its absence was not a missed local workspace tarball: it was the expected result of React's undeclared direct dependency. The package is present in the monorepo root installation (`node_modules/@fluentui/react-icons/package.json`, version 2.0.344), but that is not the isolated consumer's installation.

No evidence in this review indicates an incorrect peer classification, incomplete install of a dependency declared by React, or an export-map incompatibility.

### P1-03B Native ESM entrypoint scope audit — 2026-10-24

The authorized correction was paused before implementation after measuring the emitted package-root graph. `packages/react/src/index.ts` contains 34 relative runtime export references, all emitted without `.js` extensions. The current `packages/react/dist/index.js` therefore has more than the initial `./CyberSheet` failure: resolving its public barrel transitively reaches a broad component graph.

A static traversal of the current emitted graph from `dist/index.js`, following relative static imports/exports and resolving existing `.js` files or directory `index.js` files, found 209 reachable JavaScript modules and 421 relative specifiers. Of these, 402 are extensionless relative JavaScript specifiers in 108 importer files. The remaining 19 specifiers are CSS imports in 19 files, including ribbon styles and `components/ExcelApp.js`'s `./excel-app.css`. The traversal found no missing local JavaScript targets under bundler-style extension/index resolution. These counts describe the checked-in build output; they do not claim every module body is safe to evaluate in Node.

This is beyond a correction limited to the root barrel or a few follow-on imports. Making the full current root graph natively resolvable would require correcting hundreds of emitted specifiers across many internal modules, and separately deciding how the Node ESM entry should handle CSS that browser bundlers currently consume. Those changes meet the directive's stop condition for broad internal import rewriting or distribution-architecture expansion. **Recommended next boundary.** Before implementation, decide whether the public root barrel must remain one native-Node-loadable graph, or whether the package can expose a Node-safe root entry while retaining browser-only component exports through a separately documented/bundler entry. Under the approved Option A contract, a viable correction likely needs a build-time specifier rewrite for the React emitted JavaScript graph plus an explicit CSS distribution strategy; this is broader than changing `src/index.ts`. Any such strategy must preserve the existing browser package-root API and export names, so it may not simply omit component exports. Once that boundary is approved, use a clean emitted graph audit to enumerate and verify all rewritten relative specifiers, then run the prescribed packed Node and Vite gates. This report does not authorize that broader implementation.

### P1-03D Node ESM distribution design review — 2026-10-24

**Build and graph.** The React package currently builds with `tsc -p tsconfig.json`, then runs `scripts/package-assets.mjs`; the emitted package is an unbundled source-relative graph. The root `src/index.ts` exports 34 relative runtime targets. The traversal recorded in P1-03B found 209 reachable emitted JavaScript modules and 402 extensionless relative JavaScript specifiers across 108 importer files. These modules are currently emitted separately under `dist` and shipped by the package's `files: ["dist"]` rule. The React build itself does not bundle or rewrite runtime imports.

The package dependency graph adds constraints beyond those 402 React-local paths. `@cyber-sheet/core` is built with tsup to ESM entrypoints and its current root output has no local relative imports in the inspected entry. `@cyber-sheet/io-xlsx` is a direct dependency built with `tsc`; its emitted root barrel has extensionless exports and imports `fflate` and the Core peer. `@cyber-sheet/icons/react` resolves to raw TSX source. `@cyber-sheet/renderer-canvas` is a peer dependency whose current `tsc` output starts with extensionless exports from `dist/src/index.js`, and its internal modules also use extensionless specifiers. A React-only Node bundle that leaves this renderer peer external would still encounter a Node-resolution failure. Core and renderer are peers and should not be silently duplicated without checking their public runtime identity contracts.

| Alternative | Implementation scope | Browser compatibility | React/runtime identity | CSS | Native Node resolution | Verification burden |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One bundled ESM output replacing current output | Medium; change the package build and entry artifact | Highest risk to the accepted Vite path, file layout, source maps, and tree-shaking behavior | Can preserve host React by externalizing `react`, `react-dom`, and `react/jsx-runtime`; Core/renderer peer duplication needs explicit control | Requires a bundler rule; removing CSS from the one output would change browser styling | Removes React-local relative paths, but does not solve external peer failures by itself | High; must requalify package root, Vite, CSS, exports, and identity |
| Post-build specifier rewriting | Medium; a deterministic pack/build transform over emitted files | Preserves the current separate-file browser graph if browser output is unchanged | Naturally preserves peer identities | Does not address CSS imports | Must rewrite hundreds of React specifiers and also handle renderer/io-xlsx outputs or other package imports; raw TSX icons still need compilation; CSS still cannot be loaded as JavaScript | High; audit every rewritten target, directory index, and dependency boundary |
| Separate browser and Node targets | Medium to high; add a Node ESM target and root conditions while retaining the existing browser target | Lowest regression risk because current browser entry and copied CSS remain intact | Externalize host React and Core. Keep renderer as a peer only if its Node entry becomes resolvable; otherwise bundling it risks callback/constructor identity | Keep current CSS imports/assets on the browser condition; omit CSS imports from Node output. Publish/document a separately addressable stylesheet if Node SSR consumers need to include styles | A Node-specific bundle removes React-local paths and can bundle non-peer problematic dependencies such as icons and io-xlsx; renderer peer needs a coordinated Node-safe route or an explicit bundling/identity decision | Highest total matrix, but failures stay isolated by condition and current browser output remains available |

**CSS policy.** The 19 emitted CSS imports divide into 18 imports of `ribbon.css` from ribbon components and one `excel-app.css` import from `ExcelApp.js`. These are component styling side effects, not Node runtime code. The current helper copies the two source stylesheets to `dist/components/ribbon/ribbon.css` and `dist/components/excel-app.css`, while the browser-oriented emitted JavaScript imports them directly. The recommended Node target should exclude CSS imports only from that target; it must not remove or rewrite the browser imports/assets. A Node package import would then load without CSS, while a browser bundler continues selecting the existing browser graph and CSS imports. If SSR consumers need stylesheet delivery, document a stable stylesheet asset path and expose it deliberately; do not make native Node import attempt to evaluate CSS or silently claim server-rendered markup is styled.

**Runtime identity.** The React package declares React and ReactDOM as peers. Any Node bundle must externalize `react`, `react-dom`, and `react/jsx-runtime`, so it uses the consumer's React instance. Core is also a peer and should remain external to preserve Workbook/class identity. `renderer-canvas` is a peer and `CyberSheet` constructs its `CanvasRenderer` and exposes it through `onRendererReady`; therefore embedding a second renderer copy may change `instanceof` and constructor identity for consumers that also import the peer. The current renderer package output is not Node-resolvable, so the cleanest identity-preserving plan is a coordinated conditional Node entry for that peer, externalized by React's Node bundle. This makes the implementation boundary include a small renderer-canvas packaging change, subject to separate authorization. The React Node target can bundle or compile the non-peer raw TSX icon package and the tsc-based io-xlsx dependency; Core remains external. The current React bundle should also externalize ReactDOM's JSX runtime rather than inlining it.

**Import-time browser dependency scan.** Source inspection found browser APIs primarily in component render/handler/effect paths and in utility functions, not obvious unguarded module-scope reads. `globalConfig` checks `typeof document` before DOM work; `keyboardLayout` checks `typeof navigator` before reading `navigator.platform`; local-storage access is inside caught helper calls. `HTMLElement` uses in the component sources are predominantly type annotations and event-handler logic. Renderer construction and DOM observers occur after component mounting. This is a static inspection, not proof of Node import safety: transitive dependency evaluation must be checked in the packed Node test, and SSR render-time safety needs a separate ReactDOM server run.

**Recommendation.** Use separate browser and Node targets, with the Node target implemented as a bundled ESM entry rather than rewriting hundreds of emitted imports. Route the package root's browser condition to the current `dist/index.js` unchanged and its Node condition to a new Node ESM bundle; keep the shared declaration entry and public export set aligned. Externalize `react`, `react-dom`, `react/jsx-runtime`, and Core. Add a coordinated Node-resolvable renderer-canvas entry and externalize that peer from React's Node bundle to preserve the `onRendererReady` instance contract. Bundle the remaining non-peer React dependencies that currently expose raw TSX or extensionless tsc graphs. Exclude CSS only in the Node target, keep the two copied CSS files and current browser imports intact, and document a stable stylesheet asset for consumers that need styles with SSR. This has more packaging pieces than a rewriter, but avoids changing the qualified browser output and avoids peer duplication. It is a design recommendation only; no implementation is authorized by P1-03D.

### P1-03E Renderer Node ESM and peer-identity contract — 2026-10-24

**Renderer package and entry graph.** `packages/renderer-canvas/package.json` declares ESM, points `main` and `module` at `dist/src/index.js`, points types at `dist/src/index.d.ts`, has no `exports` conditions, and declares `@cyber-sheet/core` as a peer. Its build is only `tsc -p tsconfig.json`; `tsconfig.json` emits the source tree under `dist/src`. The emitted root barrel has 24 extensionless relative export references. A static traversal from that entry reaches 26 JavaScript modules and 41 extensionless relative specifiers across six importer files. Renderer-canvas has no CSS import in the inspected source graph. It therefore has the same Node ESM resolution defect, even though its own graph is much smaller than React's.

The renderer is used independently outside React: the package root is imported by the Vue, Svelte, and Angular integrations, examples, a vanilla test project, and documented consumer examples. Its browser/default entry must remain the current `dist/src/index.js` so those routes retain their existing resolution behavior. A Node condition can select a separate Node-safe artifact without changing the browser path.

**React-to-renderer contract.** `CyberSheet.tsx` imports the runtime `CanvasRenderer` constructor from `@cyber-sheet/renderer-canvas`, creates that class in its mount effect, stores the resulting instance, calls its methods, disposes it on cleanup, and passes that exact object to the public `onRendererReady?: (renderer: CanvasRenderer) => void` callback. The instance is therefore externally observable, and constructor identity is part of practical compatibility for consumers that also import the peer. `CanvasRenderer` is not re-exported by the React root, but it is present in the public callback type and callback value.

The `CyberSheet` implementation imports `Workbook` from the Core peer and uses its class/runtime behavior. Core identity should also remain external to the React Node bundle. Existing consumers import the renderer peer directly from Vue, Svelte, Angular, examples, and standalone usage. These are separate adapters, not proof that they share one renderer instance with React, but they establish that the renderer package root is independently public and must retain its current browser contract.

**Renderer runtime dependencies.** The renderer graph imports Core and its own relative modules; it has no React dependency and no stylesheet imports. DOM and browser APIs such as `document.createElement`, `window`, `ResizeObserver`, canvas, and event listeners appear in constructors, methods, and interaction paths. In React, the renderer constructor is called from an effect after mount. Static inspection found no obvious unguarded module-scope DOM read in the renderer entry graph, but this is not a Node import or SSR qualification. Formula-worker creation remains governed by the existing Option B behavior and is not changed by this package decision.

| Alternative | Identity behavior | Dependencies/CSS/browser behavior | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A — Coordinated Node-safe renderer entry | React's Node bundle externalizes `@cyber-sheet/renderer-canvas`; Node and direct peer imports resolve to the same conditional renderer entry and constructor. Core remains the shared external peer. | Bundle the renderer's own relative graph into a Node ESM artifact, externalize Core, and leave its current browser graph selected for bundlers. There is no renderer CSS to handle. Browser APIs remain in runtime methods/constructors; package import safety and SSR still require separate tests. | **Recommended.** Smallest option that resolves the peer's known Node failure and preserves one observable `CanvasRenderer` identity. Requires a coordinated renderer-canvas package/build change. |

With its current `tsc` graph, the React Node import still fails when it follows the external peer. | Internalizing React's non-peer problematic dependencies does not repair the renderer peer's 41 paths. Renderer has no CSS; its browser globals are deferred to runtime paths. | Not sufficient by itself. Once a Node-safe peer entry is added, this reduces to Alternative A. |

**Recommendation and implementation boundary.** Select Alternative A as the renderer/React identity architecture. Keep a conditional Node ESM bundle for React that externalizes `react`, `react-dom`, `react/jsx-runtime`, `@cyber-sheet/core`, and `@cyber-sheet/renderer-canvas`.
